speechtext: What action has the federal government taken in the province of Ontario toward preparing hospitals to operate under disaster conditions?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether it is the intention of the government to convene a meeting here in Ottawa shortly with all parties who are interested in the supply of gas to eastern Canadian markets in Ontario and Quebec, in order to arrive at a decision on that question, which is of such importance to the gas producers of the western provinces.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED CONFERENCE CONCERNING SUPPLY TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all I can say is that during the course of the preliminary meetings of the federal-provincial conference I had some conversation with the premier of Alberta who told me he was trying to organize a meeting that would take place here in Ottawa between himself and representatives of gas producers, and representatives of companies interested in providing a pipe line, to examine seriously the situation and try to determine what should be done.

Inquiries of the Ministry
I told him that I would be very glad to participate, but that I would prefer if possible that it would not be before the return to this country of Mr. Howe. He told me that it would not in any event have been convenient to have one before Mr. Howe's expected return, but that shortly after his return he would communicate with me and tell me what progress he had made toward organizing that kind of meeting.

subtopic: REPORTED CONFERENCE CONCERNING SUPPLY TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED CONFERENCE CONCERNING SUPPLY TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext: No, I cannot say that a meeting is going to be convened to determine the question once and for all. It is a meeting that the premier of Alberta had in mind to deal with a natural resource of that province, and I do not think it would be proper for us to convene a meeting for that purpose. The premier of the province is arranging for that kind of a discussion. Whether the discussion will reach a point that can be regarded as final is something that no one can predict before the meeting takes place.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 10, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday when the house adjourned I was discussing the question of family allowances, and had been quoting from Hansard for 1944. I was doing that because one hon. member had risen a day or so ago and accused members of this party of voting in 1944 against the family allowances measure which, he said, had appeared in the speech from the throne, and in other places. I had reviewed the part we had played in the debate in reply to the speech from the throne of that year, particularly as it dealt with family allowances, and I had shown from the record that Social Credit members on every occasion had agreed with the government on the principle of family allowances. I had pointed out that the fact we had voted non-confidence in the government in the division on the address in reply did not indicate at that time, nor does it ever indicate when a vote is being taken on the address, that those who voted against were voting against any suggestion made in the address.

I had pointed out that it did deal with thanks being offered the Governor General for making his address to the House of Commons.
I should like now to go one step further in connection with the discussion which took place in the budget debate of 1944. I would ask hon. members to turn to page 4377 of Hansard for June 29, 1944, where they will find recorded a quotation I should like now to place on record. It is as follows:
I was pleased to see the government do one thing; that is, institute family allowances. May I remind the Minister of Pensions and National Health that the principle of family allowances was first advocated by us; only we called it a national dividend.
I made these remarks when I spoke in the debate, as recorded at page 4377 of Hansard. In the next column I had this to say regarding family allowances on that particular occasion:
Whenever I have an opportunity to congratulate the government I am only too pleased to do so, but that seldom happens. The government has been accused of bringing in this program of family allowances as election bait, and I should like to say just a word on that point. As I have said already, I believe the principle is sound.
During the debate other hon. members suggested that the Prime Minister had brought in the family allowances as election bait because an election was in the offing. Whether or not that was the case on that occasion, sir, it seems rather a coincidence that a by-election is now taking place in Alberta. That may be the reason why the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) made the allegations he did a day or so ago regarding this question. Perhaps he had the same thought in mind, but if he has, then I am sure the facts I am placing on the record will serve a very useful purpose in acquainting the people of Canada, and particularly the people of that riding, if he intends to send his speeches out there, with the truth of the matter. I continue with the quotation:
The Prime Minister stated definitely that the measure would not come into operation until July 1, 1945, and therefore he concluded that no one could accuse him of attempting to buy votes. Just let us analyse the position. I say that the most honourable thing the Prime Minister could have done was to bring that legislation into effect right now and give the people their family allowances. As it is, what is he doing? He is holding a club over the heads of the people of Canada, and saying, in effect at least, "If you do not vote Liberal-*"
There was an interruption at that point. A little further down I had this to say:
I quite anticipated a question like that, and I shall deal with it later on. In effect, the Prime Minister is saying, "If you do not vote Liberal you will not get family allowances. If you do vote Liberal we will give them to you." I think that is the worst kind of political intrigue.

Now, Mr. Speaker, let me apply the words that I used on that occasion to the debate which took place here the other day. If this is being used as political intrigue, then it is the worst type.
I do not intend to refer any more to what I said on that occasion, but I wish to put a quotation on the record which will leave no doubt whatsoever in the mind of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, and I hope he will take this to heart. At page 5412 of Hansard of July 26, 1944, the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) spoke. I have pointed it out many times, Mr. Speaker; I have referred to the votes and I have given the actual quotations of members of this party. But I do not see how it is possible for the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek to make statements such as he did the other day that we had voted against the family allowances measure.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was just reading the remarks of the hon. member for Acadia and I shall continue them:
However, that does not mean that we are entirely satisfied with all the provisions of the bill, but

The Budget-Mr. C. E. Johnston
we will deal with them when we are in committee. Personally I am not very much impressed with most of the criticisms-
I want you to notice that, Mr. Speaker.
I am not very much impressed with most of the criticisms that have been levelled against this measure. For example, it is argued that one of the provinces will benefit to a greater extent than the others.
Of course, that reference was to the province of Quebec. I continue:
The same people charge that this is a form of appeasement to Quebec. I do not think that is a fair criticism. If the principle of the bill is sound, and I believe it is, that these allowances should be paid as a right, then what difference does it make where children may live, whether they live in the east, west or centre? As time goes on, that is a situation which may very well change. After all, it is a situation that is fully under the control of the people residing in the respective provinces. They can change it as they so desire.
I hear somebody behind me say: Page the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
This is the debate that took place on the family allowances measure itself. I want to conclude in a few minutes by referring to further paragraphs of the actual debate on family allowances when the measure came up for second reading. This is the only time throughout that entire debate, in fact throughout the entire session, when there was a vote on the family allowances measure. Of course, as was indicated in the speech from the throne during that year, the governor general indicated that a measure dealing with family allowances would be placed before us. Of course, that measure did appear and it is the one we are talking about now. The debate on second reading appears on page 5538. The vote is recorded, Mr. Speaker, and you will find that everyone in the house supported it. There was not one dissenting vote. The yeas were 139 and the nays, nil. Surely, Mr. Speaker, no one can honestly rise in his place in this house and say that the Social Crediters voted against the family allowances measure, either as it was mentioned in the speech from the throne or when it came before the house.
I have traced the history of family allowances right from the opening day of parliament in 1944 to the present. The bill was reported, read the third time and passed unanimously, as will be found on page 5757 of Hansard for the year 1944. Surely, I cannot make it any plainer than that. I have tried to outline the entire discussion on family allowances; I have traced the discussion through its various stages.
On the speech from the throne, on the budget, on the Family Allowances Act itself; at every one of those stages the Social Credit party supported the principle of family 
allowances. When the only vote on this motion was recorded the record clearly indicates that Social Credit members voted in favour of the motion. I hope that from now on, since the record has been put straight on this matter, no hon. member will dare rise in his place in this house or outside of this house and say that the Social Credit party ever voted against the family allowance measure.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) has been talking through his Social Credit hat. The question I would like to ask is this: the proposal for family allowances was contained in the speech from the throne and I should like to ask the hon. member why he voted for the defeat of the government on February 10, 1944, when he voted against the adoption of the speech from the throne which contained the family allowance proposal. If that vote had gone the other way the government would have been defeated and we would have had to depend on Social Credit for family allowances.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member has asked me a question. It seems to be the mentality of certain people that when they say they want to ask a question it is merely a deception; they have no intention of asking a question, they simply want to make another speech. The hon. member has stated that we voted against the proposal in the speech from the throne.
There was no proposal in the speech from the throne. May I once again read what the governor general said on that occasion. Are some people going to be so stupid as not to understand what the governor general said? Here are his own words:
-you will be asked to approve a measure-
That is clearly an indication that the proposal was never in the speech from the throne. How could it be? It just simply could not be. This is what the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek said in his speech as reported on page 3512 of Hansard of May 5, 1955:
-in regard to the adoption of the family allowance measure, the following names are written, and they are written there in indelible ink. There is nothing that any Social Crediter can do that will erase it. They are written there at page 364.
I say that there is no vote on page 364 of Hansard of 1944 on the family allowance measure. There is just no such vote there. The hon. member wanted me to answer his question and of course I will answer it. We never voted against the family allowance measure. We have voted non-confidence in the government and shall continue to do so

as long as they put through such measures, which result in the tremendous unemployment problem we have today.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to join this portion of the debate, but I shall do so briefly. There is not too much that I intend to add to the argument between my genial colleague, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer), and my equally genial friend, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston). Two such genial gentlemen should be able to get along a little better.
However, to make a long story short I should like to quote the opinion of a former hon. member of this house who unfortunately is now deceased. I think that this hon. member was perhaps better thought of by hon. members in every quarter of the house than almost any other member of the House of Commons. I should like to quote the words of the late Gordon Graydon as reported on page 2541 of Hansard of April 25, 1949. Referring to the very vote about which the two hon. members have been talking he had this to say:
There in Hansard on February 10, 1944, is the answer to all those things that have been said.
And again:
But you cannot drown out the nays that are recorded on page 364 of Hansard of February 10, 1944. There are the names of those who voted against the speech from the throne which contained the family allowances measure.
I do not think there was any hon. member of this house whose opinions were more highly respected than those of Gordon Graydon and that is what he said on this particular point.
There are a few other matters I should like to deal with. I just returned from a 4,500 mile trip through my riding, pretty well all within its borders, about 3,500 miles by air and about 1,000 miles by car. I think I have obtained a pretty fair cross-section of opinion as to the state of the nation in those parts.
I gathered that the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) was fairly well received. That which was received best was the resistance indicated to the terrific pressure of the past few months, not only in this house but by delegations of various kinds, to raise the tariff on incoming goods. Farmers in western Canada sell their produce on the world market and take what they can get. They do not have too great a quarrel with that, but in return they insist that they be permitted to buy on a market as nearly similar as it is possible to get, particularly that they be able to buy from those people who buy their products.
The Budget-Mr. Harrison
We have had many speeches, particularly from members of the official opposition, during this session asking for higher tariffs on British woollen goods and other goods. They get up and wrap themselves in the British flag and talk about calling a trade convention of the British commonwealth of nations.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a pretty good thing to wrap yourself up in.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You will get more of this and you had better learn to take it. That is a horse of another colour. On one occasion they talk about a trade convention of commonwealth countries but the moment old Britain sells a yard of woollen cloth under their noses they want something done about it. People in the west, and particularly the farmers in my area, are very pleased at the stand taken by the Minister of Finance in resisting that type of pressure. We are not particularly interested in buying some ersatz type of thermos bottle at twice the price just because it is made in a Conservative riding near Toronto.
The policies of the Tory party have resulted in the representation they presently have in the west. They have nothing else to thank for it. Indicative of their treatment of people in the west is the treatment recently of their leader in British Columbia. I do not agree with their leader in British Columbia in his conclusions regarding the leader of that party in this house; in fact I disagree with him entirely; but I do not think he was treated any too well. Those are the opinions he holds. After 20 years of hard labour in the province of Saskatchewan they have finally elected a Conservative member to the provincial house. Now, lo and behold, our Social Credit friends come along and are going to steal him from under their noses as their Social Credit leader; so our press is telling us.

I should like to quote to
you a great authority on this very subject, none other than our friend the premier of Saskatchewan. I shall show you that he is quite an authority on Social Credit. Wanted, an unsuccessful political figure willing to take the position of Social Credit leader in

Saskatchewan, former political affiliations unimportant. Main qualifications-willingness to do what he's told.

This is not the first time the Social Credit party in one province has endeavoured to select the leadership of the Social Credit in another province. One thing is certain: If Mr. Kohaly doesn't accept their lucrative offer he is going to make it very embarrassing for whoever does. One would be able to assume that in the meantime the price has gone up.
Mr. Douglas is a man by whose opinion we should be guided in this respect. I have read a tew of Mr. Douglas' posters for the election campaign of 1935. It is interesting to read what these posters have on them. The first says "Fletcher". I thought at first that possibly it was "Thatcher", but I see it is "Fletcher":
Fletcher is not a Social Credit candidate.
Signed-H. W. Arnold, Social Credit provincial organizer, Saskatoon, Sask.
C.P.R. telegram.

Sept. 30, 1935.
Rev. T. C. Douglas,
Weyburn, Sask.
This will confirm endorsation of convention held Weyburn, twenty-eighth, of you as Social Credit candidate.

Underneath that it says: "Vote Douglas". At the bottom it says "Issued by the C.C.F.- Social Credit, Weyburn Federal Constituency." The C.C.F. will make the Social Credit scheme possible." Either the battles we have had between the two groups in this house are just so much window dressing or this poster means what it says. Vote Douglas
Issued by the C.C.F.-Social Credit, Weyburn Federal Constituency.
While he was here recently, Premier Bennett from British Columbia made some bombastic speeches to the effect that this small group was going to take over the federal government in the next election.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you getting worried?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I am not a bit afraid. You can concentrate on my riding if you want to. Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record what has happened to some of these gentlemen in other places. Here I might interject something that I learned from

my hon. colleague from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), who is a man of long experience here. He said, "When the balloon is large, you provide the pin." I propose to provide the pin right now. You will find an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of the 15th November, 1954, which gives an indication as to how this party is doing in other places. It refers to the recent election in New Zealand, when they were also of the same opinion as Mr. Bennett, that they were going to take over there. This editorial reads as follows:
The National party, which promised little except a continuation of its moderate policies of free enterprise, won 43 out of the 80 seats in the next parliament. The Labour party, which promised some tax reductions and increases in welfare benefits was successful in the other 37 seats. The Social Credit party, which promised the voters everything but the moon with a fence around it, failed to get a single candidate elected.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: I believe that if the hon. gentleman paid closer attention to what I said he would not be making the interjection he is making. If he has any troubles, he can come around and see me and I shall fix him up. There may be a question by hon. members as to what stopped Social Credit from coming across the border into Saskatchewan over such a long period of years. It is not because it has not tried. Of course, many hon. members are familiar with the iron curtain, and some are familiar with the bamboo curtain. But we have a curtain on the border of Saskatchewan that is known as the pussywillow curtain. It may not be important to you people, but it is important to the people of Saskatchewan. As you know, the Social Credit machine runs on oil, and this pussywillow is a very sticky proposition-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You hope.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You hope.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The result has been that this pussywillow curtain has worked both ways. The socialists have stubbed their toes on the roots of this innocent-looking shrub and have fallen headlong into the province of Alberta also. I do not want to confine my remarks to my hon. friends over here, as we have even worse troubles in Saskatchewan.
The Budget-Mr. Harrison
In my trip I discovered that our friends of the, shall we say, left and the far left, who are in power in Saskatchewan at the moment, are suffering some falling-off in their prestige. There are reasons for this. This fact has been apparent in the northern part of Saskatchewan and the part that I represent because there they have applied socialism to the resources of the province most rigorously. It has not affected the people farther south so much. Now larger municipal units in that area have been rammed down people's throats without any vote. The hottest political issue I ran into when I was home was the proposed compulsory marketing of livestock. In my riding there is a tremendous resistance to that system, although Mr. Douglas says it is going to come. The downfall of the C.C.F. government is not too far away.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have been saying that for a long time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The main reason for that is the high taxation they have imposed on the land in Saskatchewan. Around Meadow Lake it is about four times what it was when they took office, and under present economic conditions out there it amounts to being confiscatory.
Finally, the pro-red tendencies of this party which finally came out in this session, and which have been indicated by actions taken by some of their members recently in this house, also are coming home to roost. Hence the party has slipped considerably in the last little while.
I should now like to take you briefly, Mr. Speaker, on a run around the little riding that I represent and give you some idea of the problems that are presented to you, and the variety of them that can be presented in a 3,500-mile trip by air in a riding that occupies nearly all of the north of the province, an area running 500 miles north and south and 250 miles east and west along the border of the Northwest Territories on one side, Alberta on the other and there is only a 60-mile strip of land in between my eastern border and Manitoba. This riding occupies about 40 per cent of the province of Saskatchewan. Being an area of 500 miles in length, running north and south, there is naturally quite a great deal of difference in the economy at the north end from that at the south end. In the southern end you are in an agricultural area. The agriculture is largely of a mixed-farming variety. In the middle you have timber and other natural resources such as fur and fishing. In the north you get into the great Canadian shield where mineral development has just been

The Budget-Mr. Harrison commenced but is already on a tremendous scale. Possibly if I took you from one little place to another, and just gave you an idea of what kind of problems you ran into in this area, Mr. Speaker, it would give you some idea of the size of the riding.
My first stop was at Meadow Lake, which is my main market town, about 80 miles north of the southern border. There I attended a meeting of the board of trade and they told me what problems they had. The first problem was an airfield so they could communicate with the large mineral area at lake Athabasca. I was able to assure them that the federal government was going to give them assistance this year in that respect and that work would commence on it this year.
The next problem they had, of course, was the flooding of Meadow lake and this was previous to the storms that have just occurred in Saskatchewan. Meadow lake itself had backed up about 30 miles to South Makwa and much land that previously has been cultivated will not be possible to cultivate this year. The Beaver river, which is usually about 75 yards wide, was some 14 miles or 15 miles wide for distances of 50 miles or 60 miles. I was speaking to one farmer there. I asked him how things were going in that country. This was previous to the recent flooding because they have had three bad storms there since then. He said, "My old man lost about 50 head of whitefaces that went down the river". I said, "Has he got any left?" He said, "Oh yes, he has a few. Some he took off the islands. When it flooded last year he was not able to get them off until December on account of the ice being thin and the fall being mild".
This is an indication of the kind of thinking that you get in that part of the country. These people were pioneers and they still have the pioneering spirit. They do not run to the nearest government with their troubles. They look after a great many of them themselves. It is not that they do not have troubles. But with all this flooding, I have not had one communication from Meadow Lake, and it is just as hard hit as is any other place in Saskatchewan. That is a tribute to the type of thinking in that part of the country. The main thing that they want-particularly from their experience over the last 10 years-is as little interference from government as possible. That has been their trouble.
I was able to charter an aeroplane, I might say, in Meadow Lake, and we took off for Green Lake, 35 miles east. The troubles we ran into there were that the provincial government had talked the metis into relinquishing their land and had given them in return

a 33-year lease. Having done that, they proceeded to take the timber off it and they said that now belongs to the provincial government. This left the metis without much means of support because it was on timber and lumber that they had depended in years gone by.
At Beauval, 100 miles north, where there is an Oblate mission which has been there for many years, the problem there was the payment to trappers and fishermen of compensation by the dominion government for loss of their fishing and hunting grounds taken over by the Cold Lake bombing range. Going further to lle-a-la-Crosse, the problem of the bombing range was about the same. They also required a new wharf as the present one is so dilapidated that it cannot be used at all. Most of their freight comes via water, and this is greatly needed.
Then I come to Buffalo Narrows, which is quite a fishing centre in the middle of Saskatchewan, situated on the Churchill and Peter Pond lakes, two of the large lakes in the Churchill river chain. Buffalo Narrows, I might say, is a fishing point that produces and processes over half the commercial fish caught within the province of Saskatchewan. There I ran into a small problem. Two war veterans wanted their veterans grant to go into the mink raising business. I found that the main topic of conversation there was the new policy with regard to mink raising in that area, which is proposed by the minister of resources in the province of Saskatchewan, Mr. Brockelbank.
It might be well for me to quote what the old policy was. The old policy was that the fish allowance was based on political expediency, and in the Churchill lake area and Buffalo Narrows, the mink raisers were limited to a catch of rough fish for their mink of 1J to 2 million pounds but they were carefully selected, and particularly before an election. Any mink raiser who showed a tendency to vote against the present government in Saskatchewan, although he might have 1,500 mink on hand and naturally required fish with which to feed them, was suddenly cut in his fishing rights to requirements for 300 or 400 mink. He was thus forced, maybe in the summertime, when the mink fur would have no commercial value, either to dispose of them to a party adherent who could get fishing rights, or to let them die. This policy has been changed and when Mr. Brockelbank made the announcement of the change he said that as a result of research in the area it was found that instead of the lakes being able to support mink on a catch of 2 million pounds of rough fish the lake could quite easily sustain a catch of 7 million

pounds of fish for the use of mink. This caused considerable amusement amongst the mink raisers because they found that Mr. Brockelbank's policy was mainly contingent on a policy formulated in Newfoundland by one Joseph Smallwood. Now, the mink raising policy in Saskatchewan is being run by remote control from Newfoundland. Mr. Smallwood ran advertisements in the newspapers in Saskatchewan asking the mink raisers there to go to Newfoundland and he would pay all the expenses of moving them and their equipment. There would be no monkey business about licences for fishing, and they would have adequate supplies of fish. Two or three of them did move out of the district and the net result was that Mr. Brockelbank found his department had done a lot of research and ascertained the lake would support many more mink. The mink raisers were happy about this because they know that in the future their licences will not be revoked, leaving them up in the air with a lot of mink that they cannot feed.
The next point from Buffalo Narrows was Cree lake. It is 150 miles northeast of Buffalo Narrows and about 275 miles northeast of Meadow Lake. It is a fisherman's paradise, well known to United States fishermen who come up to catch lake trout, giant muskies, and Arctic grayling which abound in that lake. The problem at that point may seem a little strange to eastern members since it related to the mail service. They asked for a once a month or once every two months service. At the moment the residents have to go to Buffalo Narrows, 150 miles away or 300 miles for the round trip to get their mail. I am therefore sometimes somewhat amused by members complaining to the Post Office Department because their mail is not delivered twice a day instead of once.
At Black lake, which is 130 miles north of Cree lake and just east of the east end of lake Athabasca, a problem was put before me by the Chipewyan Indian band. They wanted a portable sawmill to be used by the mission at Black Lake to make lumber for the erection of buildings for their own use. The power for it would be supplied by the mission tractor, and the resident priest, who is an expert sawyer, assured me they could make very good lumber and I am sure they could. The chief of the tribe, a gentleman by the name of Chicken, was exercised over the fact that the people from the United States were coming into the area in larger numbers every year to fish for grayling and were forcing the Indians from some of their traditional camp and fishing sites. He had no objection to these people coming 50433-232
The Budget-Mr. Harrison there to fish, but he would like some legal status for the Indians set up by this government that would entitle them to a small acreage that had been traditionally theirs, and the various sites around the lake which they have always used. It seemed to me this would be a wise provision.
There was a problem, too, with regard to a school for the children. Recently the mission granted the use of their building to start the school in operation, and no doubt a school will be built there.
At Stony lake, just west of Black lake, the problem was an outbreak of flu. I was not able to do anything about that.
At Stony Rapids, which is at the extreme east end of lake Athabasca, there is an air base and a future power site. They had no problems whatever, so that was a good spot for a politician to be.
Fond-du-lac, 100 miles west on the north shore of lake Athabasca, has been a Hudson's Bay Company trading post for about 100 years. The mission has been there nearly as long. A new modern mission and a large four-room school were built there last year. The problem there concerned a dock because the very rugged terrain on the north shore of lake Athabasca makes it nearly impossible to land goods or people there. They wanted a small dock so they could dock planes or barges and embark or debark people and goods.
Now, we come to Uranium City and the Beaver lodge area. This is something I wanted to include in my remarks particularly because some newspaperman who usually writes articles for the Saskatchewan provincial government was in there last winter, and for some reason or other came out with the idea that this area was going backward. He gave it considerable publicity of an adverse nature. I have been going into that area yearly since 1944, and sometimes twice a year. The first organized search for uranium started there in 1949. Since then, in my opinion, there has been a tremendous development. I see it every year. In 1953 when the federal mine came into operation and the $20 million 750 ton a day mill went into operation, there were real signs of the progress that has taken place. I went over this mill thoroughly on a couple of occasions including this trip.
The mill employs about 750 men, and the manager tells me that from his experience, which covers some 40 years in the various provinces of Canada, for every man employed in the mine or mill about four other people will be employed in the district. With other mines coming into production in that area,

The Budget-Mr. Harrison he tells me the result will be that at least 15,000 people will be working in the area within the next two years. He also told me that there are already 120 million tons of high grade ore proven in the area.
I flew from there about 20 miles south to the new Gunnar mine. This is something that is hard to believe unless you see it. Eighteen months ago, it was nothing but wilderness on a point of land which jutted out into lake Athabasca. A year and a half ago there was nothing there, but now there is a commercial empire consisting mainly of a $25 million plant covering many acres which will be in production by the middle of August. In order to give you some idea of the size of this new plant, I may say that the power for it is produced by a diesel electric plant. This diesel plant will produce more electrical energy than the proposed South Saskatchewan dam. The Gunnar mill works on an acid process because their ore is a little different from that at Eldorado mine about 20 miles north. They have put up their own sulphuric acid plant which occupies about half a city block. The pile of sulphur alongside it is about 80 feet high and half a block long. They have built their own new hospital, and I am told that they poured 10,000 cubic yards of concrete there last fall in a month and a half. This will give you some idea of the magnitude of this undertaking. Gunnar has a mill that will produce 1,250 tons a day in its original form, and is quite easily expandable. Only the chemical process has to be expanded. The rock crushing process is adequate to cover an output of 2,000 tons per day. The federal mine is also so designed, and will likely be extended shortly, to handle 1,500 tons a day. There are many other mines in the area. These are private mines, some of which are in production. These are Lorado, National Explorations, Rix, Nicholson and Nesbitt LaBine. There are 70 or 80 others in various stages of development. I might say that Lorado has run into enough ore that they will put up a $5 million or $6 million mill.
I was given the opportunity to hear the complaints in that district, when I attended a meeting of the board of trade, and also a Kiwanis dinner. These were as follows:
1.	That they required a federal custom mill to handle ore of the smaller mines. I asked what it would require, and they said they would need one having a daily capacity of 1,500 tons.
2.	The facilities of the army signals at Uranium are not adequate either in personnel or in equipment to handle the heavy air traffic at that point. They say that the private plane radio band is not guarded and tuned

in for signals from such planes. I intend to take that matter up with the Department of Transport.
3.	They complain of inadequate staff for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to cover a new frontier area of this size. There are two men during the daytime and one man at night. It will be recalled that there have been some outbreaks of lawlessness in the district in the last while, and these people think they should have more adequate police protection from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
4.	They ask for immediate over-all planning by the provincial government of the road system, sewers and water system, and other services such as hospitals, schools and communications, to prevent a hodge-podge of small communities at various mine sites. This was exercising them quite a lot. Many of the mine managers thought that Saskatchewan was more backward, as a province, in coming to the aid of mining, than any province in which they had operated. It appeared to them that, the way provincial authorities operated, they did not want mines there at all.
5.	They ask for the elimination of the provincial education tax on mine development material, and point out that this is very important. Making a computation of what they contributed to the education tax last year in the province they found that it amounted to about $2 million in that little area, alone. In other words they provided about one-sixth of the education tax moneys being raised in Saskatchewan, and were not getting much in return.
6.	They asked for the enactment of new labour laws by the Saskatchewan provincial government to replace those now in effect, which were described by the mine union as the worst in Canada.
7.	They asked for the completion of Saskatchewan highway No. 4 from 40 miles north of Meadow Lake to lake Athabasca, to open up further mine territory and provide communication with their own province of Saskatchewan. In this connection I would join the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Hellyer) who spoke last night and suggested a contribution by the federal government- or, even better, operation by the federal government-of a system of federal highways. Unless some foresight is shown, similar to that which was shown when the Canadian Pacific Railway was pushed across western Canada, this area will lag in its development. This is a storehouse of Canada. That area, and the Northwest Territories, comprise a storehouse of minerals, so far as Canada is concerned. Some foresight must be used in

developing this area, not only for the advantage of those who live there but for all the people in Canada. That is a place to which our expanding population can go, and where people can reside happily.
One would be surprised to see just how modern some of these northern communities are. It was my privilege to go as far north as the north shore of Great Slave lake, and to visit Yellowknife. I was impressed by the modern buildings in which these people live. The same applies of course to the mines at Beaverlodge. The people there live under modern conditions. The wages, naturally, are high. It is my view that those gentlemen who are concerned about what will happen to the coal miners should look to this area. It is a country where an outlet could be found for the energies of those miners. A north-south highway in the lake Athabasca area would give them connection with their own province. At the present time they cannot get into the ordinary commercial areas of Saskatchewan.
Then, the last suggestion:
8.	They ask for the extension of the Canadian National Railways line from Lynn Lake around the north shore of lake Athabasca to the Uranium-Beaverlodge area to open up the richest mineral storehouse in Canada.
This may sound fantastic, but stranger things have been done. It may require a couple of hundred miles of railway line, but it would open areas having tremendous timber and mineral resources.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I have occupied the time of the house long enough, and I am pleased to have had this opportunity to place my remarks on record, setting out what these people would like to have done.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am aware of the fact, as I was in business for many years, and I recognize that trade names usually mean something. I know that the word "Thermos" on a thermos bottle indicates to me that it is a better bottle than any other on the market, coming either from Japan or from my hon. friend's riding. That also applies to many other products bearing trade names. People buy those articles because they find that, by and large, they do not get stung when they purchase products having trade names. I believe that answers my hon. friend's question.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in listening to the
5,0433-232i
The Budget-Mr. Bryson
discourse of the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) when he said that he had travelled 3,500 miles by aeroplane. I do not doubt that he could travel that distance in his constituency. The only comment I would make after listening to him is that possibly he flew too high, and found himself up in a rarefied atmosphere.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At 5,000 feet.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
His great knowledge of provincial affairs has led me to the belief that possibly he has his eye on the leadership of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan. Certainly one could draw that conclusion from what he said this afternoon. However, I do not think any C.C.F.'er need worry much in Saskatchewan about any serious opposition from the Liberal party in that province. We have had a pretty good indication this afternoon, from the two speeches of Libera] members from Saskatchewan, as to what chance they have out there. Those speeches certainly just drove another nail in the coffin of the Liberal party in that province.
On two occasions yesterday two hon. members spoke somewhat briefly about conditions as they exist in that province at the present time. For a few moment only, this afternoon I should like to say something on the disaster that has occurred in that province during the past few days. I might say at the outset that the feeling of fear and concern over the possibilities of a crop being sown in Saskatchewan has been growing during the past few weeks. However, the storm of last week has left little speculation as to what the prospects from now on are going to be in respect to harvesting a normal crop in that province. It is a fact that we cannot ignore. Even before there has been any final assessment of the damage, we can take it from the best authorities that it is the worst single disaster that has ever happened there, and, for that matter, the worst single disaster that has ever happened in any province in the Dominion of Canada. We speak of "Hurricane Hazel" and "Hurricane Edna". I would suggest that "Hurricane Hazel" and "Hurricane Edna" combined were by comparison just minor disturbances. The estimates of the damages of those two hurricanes were $21 million. Just a glance at what has happened out in Saskatchewan by people who have made a casual survey leads them to believe that the damage will exceed $50 million. The estimate will be much higher, I am sure, when the final assessment is made.
The night before last I spoke over the telephone to a party in Regina who told me that the Qu'Appelle valley was flowing from bank to bank, something which I am sure had

The Budget-Mr. Bryson never occurred before in the memories of oldtimers. Preliminary estimates, as was mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), made by Professor Harrington show that the crop damage will be 50 per cent. By that I mean that 50 per cent of the crops that normally would be sown in all probability will not be sown. Except in one or two isolated areas such as Rosetown and Kindersley, the damage is very widespread. The statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he arrived back from his recent trip, that Saskatchewan has never lost a crop in May, was very unfortunate. That is the kind of statement we expect to hear from some hon. members but certainly not from a responsible minister such as the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
One of the most serious aspects is this. All of the crop that will be sown from now on-and incidentally, since the report was made that I mentioned, one inch of rain has fallen in Saskatchewan, adding to the very gloomy and dismal picture out there-will be in coarse grains. The wheat that will be sown will be late. In all probability it will be rusted as it was a year ago. Agricultural scientists tell us now that rust spores survived the winter in the southern states, and in all probability a late crop once again will be affected, with the exception of coarse grains and the very small amount of Selkirk wheat that will be sown.
It is very difficult at this stage-I am the first one to admit it-to estimate what the damage in the final analysis will amount to. To give the house some idea of how terrible it is, in the report that I received from there yesterday municipal officials say that throughout the whole of central and northern Saskatchewan the water is flowing in unheard of directions. It is running in directions that it had never run before. Roads are impassable. That was mentioned yesterday. In many places the water is running eight feet deep over the highways. In the town of Humboldt, in my own constituency, in the past two weeks people have been travelling around by boat and on foot. Not one bushel of grain has been taken to an elevator in the last two weeks. That is a very serious situation. Farmers in the Meadow Lake area, in the area of the hon. member who has just spoken, have been able to travel from Leask to Blaine Lake, a distance of 18 miles across country, in a motorboat, something before unheard of. Losses of livestock are heavy. At Meadow Lake one farmer has already lost over 500 head of cattle. Feed is scarce. Even if feed were available they cannot transport it over the roads,

which is a very serious situation indeed. Similar conditions prevail in all but the one or two isolated areas I mentioned a moment ago, particularly the Kindersley area. Certainly such a condition is disastrous, but when we stop to realize that last year we had a crop failure in Saskatchewan and combine that fact with conditions today, we have something that is more than a disaster. We must view it not only from the point of view of the Saskatchewan farmer; we must view this disaster from the effect it will have on the whole economy of Canada.
Only a few weeks ago in his budget speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) said that three-quarters of the drop in the gross national product was caused by the crop failure in western Canada last year. Think of what it is going to mean this year to the gross national product under the conditions that I have outlined. In view of this, I make this suggestion. For every acre of land that will be taken out of production because of land flooding the dominion government should make a payment of not less than $10. I do not care what they use for the cut-off date. They could say that land that is not sown after the first day of June will qualify. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act officials are now in the field and they could easily make the necessary surveys. I make that suggestion in spite of the statement of the Prime Minister yesterday in reply to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that any consideration that will be given will be given in lieu of the damage to public property in that province. I hope he will reconsider that statement in the light of this very great disaster.
Public damage has been severe. I am not going to speak of it at this time. It was dealt with at length yesterday by the hon. member for Saskatoon. Power lines, telephone lines, utilities of all kinds, municipal culverts, roads and so forth all need repairs. However, while property damage is a considerable factor and of great concern to those who lost their houses, and so on, the most important factor is the loss of farm income. It is necessary that payments be made in lieu of those losses if farmers are to carry on until another harvest.
Last year, the Saskatchewan crop was cut by 36 per cent. However, by lowering living standards, by extending their credit to the very limit, they were able to carry on. They were able to hang on in the hope that they would secure a normal crop this year and thereby be able to recoup their losses.
As I said a moment ago, the crop that will be sown after a week or so will be

coarse grains. I can imagine the Minister of Agriculture saying it can be fed to hogs. I know he will also say that farmers in Saskatchewan are in a preferred position because hog production is up 26 per cent this year over last year. I would point out to hon. members that our farmers are not going to pull themselves out of any financial difficulties by feeding barley to hogs. Barley is sown because it will mature a little earlier, but if it cannot be sold as grain it will have to be used or sold as feed for hogs.
I have here a report which indicates that early in April the hog-barley ratio at Winnipeg was about 16-3. This means that 100 pounds of live B1 hog was only equal in value to 16-3 bushels of No. 1 feed barley. A year ago 100 pounds of the same kind of hog would buy 30-5 bushels of barley. Or to make another calculation, the hog-feed margin, which is the difference in value between 21 bushels of feed value and a 150-pound hog carcass, stood at $10.45 early in April this year while a year ago it was $31.96.
I should like to make two other suggestions. I submit that it is absolutely imperative that the balance of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act payments be made at this time. To date 10 per cent of the farmers have yet to receive 40 per cent of that payment. I submit it is necessary that this payment be made with the utmost dispatch in order to alleviate 'the acute distress which is being suffered by Saskatchewan farmers because of recent flood damage. I would suggest also that the Department of Trade and Commerce make the final wheat payment immediately as this would help in this great emergency.
Far and beyond these payments, there is need for further assistance along the lines I have just suggested, with the dominion government paying not less than $10 per acre for land which will be taken out of production because of flooding. I feel that we are justified in asking for this, as in my opinion the request is a fair one. Workers in other industries are eligible for unemployment insurance benefits when they are out of work. These benefits are made available to augment their income when they are not working. The government is also giving consideration to making payments over and above these benefits when the unemployment insurance has been exhausted.
I certainly feel that $10 per acre is fair. It falls far short, and necessarily so if we are going to be fair about it, of the value of even a subnormal crop. As I say, this would be of great help in alleviating the present distress being experienced by farmers in Saskatchewan. I feel that the question of making payments for unseeded crops due to
The Budget-Mr. Schneider flooding will have to be considered next fall by the P.F.A.A. officials. I do not think the government will be able to put off making these payments, as they did last year. They will have to face up to the problem next fall in any event, but why delay? I realize that there will have to be an amendment to the act, but why delay making these payments? They should be paid now when they are needed most and when they will do the greatest good.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must speak to this house on one part of the problem of unemployment which concerns many of my constituents who have spent the best part of their lives in the manufacture of two commodities, supplying most of Canada's needs in the past and exporting millions of dollars worth to other countries. They have made a great contribution to Canada's prosperity and growth in the past and are now facing an economic situation which, in the one product, has reduced Canadian production of rubber soled canvas footwear from a high of over six million pairs in 1947 to less than two million pairs in 1954. Exports have dropped to a fraction of normal because of competition from other countries with low wage production costs, such as Hong Kong.
The loss of our exports can be expected and understood by our rubber workers, but it is another matter when the low wage cost producers are allowed to ship unlimited quantities into Canada at prices which are a fraction of the Canadian cost. In 1954 these low cost imports supplied 35 per cent of the Canadian requirements in rubber canvas footwear. The records show a steady increase of imports which closely follows the corresponding figures of decline in Canadian production.
The imports from Hong Kong are the most serious, amounting to 717,202 pairs in 1954. We are informed by the assistant Canadian trade commissioner at Hong Kong that rubber footwear factories in that district pay wages ranging from 45 to 75 cents per day, according to the 1952 report, while our Canadian rubber workers received $1.40 per hour. The duty of 27J per cent charged on such low cost products is of very little assistance, and I am not suggesting any increase in tariff. A pair of rubber canvas shoes made in Canada have a manufacturing cost of from $2 to $2.50, while Hong Kong shoes are being laid down in Canada at 65 cents per pair plus duty of 27J per cent and 10 per cent sales tax. With a total imported price of 89-4 cents per pair they are being sold in Canada by leading retailers at $1.95 per pair. Defenders of the importation of these

The Budget-Mr. Schneider low standard of living goods are inclined to quote costs in Hong Kong dollars, and do not mention the fact that a Hong Kong dollar is worth 17 Canadian cents.
Our Canadian workmen are willing to meet any fair competition, but this is not competition; it is sabotage. We can easily imagine the standard of living available to a worker on 45 to 75 cents per day, and we ask you to compare this with $1.40 per hour and the Canadian standard of living of which we are all so proud. Until recently we have heard the argument that these low cost shoes were of poor quality, but I assure you that the samples I have seen appear to be of quite good quality and are plainly marked "Made in Hong Kong".
The loss of employment to the rubber workers is only a part of the loss to Canadian workingmen, as we also lose the production of the canvas fabric, the steel eyelets, chemicals, reclaimed rubber, laces and shoe findings as well as packaging materials. While this alarming invasion of over 700,000 pairs of canvas rubber shoes in one year has already thrown hundreds of Canadians out of work-a loss of half a million hours of work-this probably is only the beginning. Canvas rubber shoes are a sideline in Canadian factories, and are produced in slack periods between the seasonal demands for waterproof footwear such as boots, rubbers, and galoshes. These waterproof lines now enter Canada free of duty under the British preferential tariff, and British footwear is making some headway in our domestic market because of wages much lower than ours. The alarming angle to the Hong Kong problem is the steady growth of their sales in Canada, and the fact that there is nothing to prevent them entering the waterproof lines and eliminating our entire rubber footwear industry.
The other problem of my people is the slow but sure elimination of the button manufacturing industry in Canada. For 85 years the largest of my three factories has served Canada, and at one time had a substantial export business. The export business has been lost to low cost competition. This factory is one of the last to be manufacturing in Canada. Competition from other countries has been serious in our remaining domestic business, but the unkindest cut of all comes in the recent invasion of so-called United States buttons which we find are shipped from New York, but are actually manufactured in Puerto Rico. The wage in this industry in Puerto Rico, I am advised, is 30 cents per hour. There is nothing fair about such competition and the Canadian buyer

naturally assumes that the buttons are made by workmen in the United States where wages are higher than ours.
This industry has served Canada well, but the staff in this surviving factory has been reduced to one-third of its former strength. If this cut-rate invasion by Puerto Rico buttons continues the skill and experience of many years will be lost to Canada. If the time should come again when we are forced to depend on our own resources, we will surely be buttonless. We have been told that the Canadian manufacturer should pull up his socks, but if we find ourselves without buttons we may have difficulty keeping our trousers up. Of course there is always the safety pin and the shingle nail.
These two problems do not call for tariff revisions for protection, nor have I ever asked for higher duty on any foreign competition on the domestic market. These two items call for a realistic consideration of standards of living. This is unfair competition between two ways of life. Are we to assume that the importers, the defenders of this unfair competition, favour the Hong Kong way of life with a bowl of rice a day and a bamboo shack, with wages of 45 to 75 cents per day, as compared to Canadian wages of $1.40 per hour? Or do they favour the Puerto Rican 30 cents per hour against the Canadian $1.20 per hour?
I am very proud to quote in this parliament advice which was given by my father, the hard-working founder of our business. He said the one sure thing in this life was change, and the difficulty was to meet these changes and adjust our lives to them. Canada is rapidly changing from a full agricultural economy to an industrial economy. This is the machine age. Are we to become a self-contained country like the United States, which has become the wealthiest country in the world, and so independent that she buys from us only when it suits her?
Anyone finding fault with our system should also find a solution, and I would suggest that we exercise the escape clauses in our GATT agreements, just as the United States and other countries do when serious injury is caused to home industry. We could place quotas on imports which threaten the existence of our producers.
I realize that trade is a two-way street, and that we must export our wheat, paper, minerals and many other products of our vast natural resources. But we must also remember that it would be unpopular to take our thousands of unplaced job applicants and put them to work growing more wheat, making more paper, digging more gold and producing more surpluses. These industrial

workers cannot remain unemployed much longer, and on their behalf I appeal for a realistic consideration of this unfair invasion of our domestic markets.
