speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Mang party in Great Britain is a habitual smoker. Few pictures were ever released in which we did not see Sir Winston with his favourite stogie either in the corner of his mouth or in his hand.
Sir Winston did not smoke steadily until after the death of his father, Lord Randolph Churchill, who died on January 24, 1895 . . . One day his father had said to him, through a haze of cigarette smoke, "Why begin to smoke? If you wish to have an eye that is true and a hand that does not quiver, if you wish never to ask yourself a question as you ride for a fence, don't smoke." Sir Winston adored his father, at a distance, and followed his advice for the time being. Happily he did not continue to do so; if he had, he would never have had a 41st birthday or been prime minister. When he was serving in France with the Scots Greys in 1915 he forgot his matches one day at the front and went back to his dugout for them. A German shell fell where he would have been if he had been a non-smoker.
Exports of tobacco in 1954 to the United Kingdom amounted to 25,184,852 pounds; exports to other countries amounted to 6,585,394 pounds, or total exports of 31,770,246 pounds. If the 3-cent reduction requested had been granted, the growers would have been in a more favourable position to export greater quantities of tobacco.
The production of flue-cured tobacco and its processing into a consumer product is an industry by which a great part of the people in the tobacco-growing districts live. It is also the main support of numerous local industries and services which manufacture, sell or service materials and machines for the tobacco industry. Merchants, garages, service stations, banks, legal firms, insurance, real estate and other businesses have gained much from the tobacco industry. It is also the largest customer of the companion branches of agriculture in these same districts. The tobacco industry may also be found to be the largest single source of tax revenue, if not in the country at least in many municipalities. Tobacco is the hub of a great wheel of local industry may also be found to be the largest sure of dependency, their fortunes rising and falling according to the state of the tobacco industry.
It is, therefore, most necessary that we should direct our thoughts and actions toward maintaining the tobacco industry in as healthy a condition as possible. Therefore I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he has failed to give adequate consideration to the 3-cent reduction on a pack of 20 cigarettes which had been asked by the flue-cured tobacco association of Ontario for the last two or three years.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to detain the house for any great length of time on this occasion, but recent events which have taken place in
[Mr. McBain.l
Saskatchewan and in my constituency of Qu'Appelle make me feel that I would be remiss in my duty if at this time I did not give some picture, so far as I am able to do so, of the latest disaster to hit us. It seems that Canada, in the last few years, has been subject to severe punishment from the weather. In 1948 we had the Fraser river flood which affected so many farmers in British Columbia, as well as towns and villages. Then we had "Hurricane Hazel" and "Hurricane Edna". We have had violent storms in Newfoundland. We in Saskatchewan now are suffering our second severe blow in succession dealt us by the weather.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In some parts four.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In some places four and five. It is not my purpose to review the vagaries of the weather but rather to point out that, in this gloomy picture that Saskatchewan has been presenting to the rest of Canada, the constituency of Qu'Appelle has been quite as severely dealt with as have other areas in Saskatchewan. Indeed, on the speech from the throne, when I had occasion to make a few remarks, I pointed out that the eastern third of the area has been suffering now for three years-in some spots for four years- owing to excessive moisture.
As many hon. members here realize, our topography, the lay of the land, is level. When you read about floods in rivers of Saskatchewan, that does not tell the whole story. The greatest disasters are not on the river banks. The disaster extends over the farm lands. The difficulty we have in that level country is that you will find dry spots where seeding could be done, but you simply cannot get on to those dry spots in order to seed them. Some two years ago, southwest of Regina, in those plains east of Wilcox and Tyvan in the southern part of the constituency, when the heavy rains came which flooded a great part of that country, many farmers actually went out, got caught in the rain and hurried home with the tractor, and the seed drill was still in the field in the middle of the summer. The havoc that such storms can cause on the level plains is hardly believable.
In the eastern third of Qu'Appelle constituency-and this applies to the constituencies north and south

we have been suffering for three years. We have made some effort- the provincial department of agriculture has done so as well, and the municipalities have struggled with the problem-to drain that water away. What is happening there is not the immediate result of saturating the ground with water now. What is happening in that part of the area is the deterioration of the topsoil owing to the fact that the water which

soaks down into the ground, when evaporation takes place, begins to come up through the land. As that process goes on it is souring the top six to ten inches of soil, bringing up the alkali and other salts. Unless definite moves are made to drain that area properly the productive value of that soil is going to be destroyed, and it will take years to retrieve.
We live in a pioneer area where some of our grandfathers are still living. They took that land over when it was raw prairie, and they built a productive empire out of it. They are still imbued with the pioneering spirit, and they do the best they can as individuals and as municipalities, but the situation has gone beyond that stage. As I said before, I do not want to go into details at this time but merely desire to present a general picture. Actually the full impact of the heavy rains and snows on this saturated soil has not been felt as yet by the people in general. While it is true that you can seed wheat up to the 24th of May and even later, nevertheless with the ground saturated as it is now a mere quarter inch of rain, for example, will stop you from going back on the land for a week or so.
I just want to emphasize this situation, not from the point of view of being an' alarmist or adopting a panicky attitude, because we have gone through periods of adversity before. As I say, our pioneers were used to having nothing 60 years ago, and they have built up the economy to the point where it is today. They have a great deal of patience, and they are great gamblers as well. They are willing to make the best of it, but the situation is such that there will have to be some positive and quick action with respect to draining these areas.
I should like to read excerpts from three letters. I am not going to read the entire letters. They are from councillors and reeves in our area. I shall quote one paragraph in this letter from Mr. James G. Duthie of Wolseley, to indicate the general situation. The pictures you saw in the newspapers the other day were of the town of Wolseley. This has to do with the farm land there. He said:
I will state briefly that there is a great deal of damage by floods within this municipality to roads, bridges and highways. Quite a lot of the farm lands in the municipality will be unfit for cultivation for years or until some drainage scheme is put into action.
There is another letter from a place farther east, and again I am going to quote briefly:
I can see no hope in trying to make a living here and pay expenses if some of this water is not drained away. There are several hundred acres covered with water. In most cases the prairie that is left isn't sufficient to feed the stock. I have been speaking to several farmers around and unless
The Budget-Mr. Mang
something can be done to get rid of this surplus water, we will have to dispose of our stock and move out.
Further down he says:
We have had this area surveyed by the department of agriculture-
That is of Saskatchewan, with the assistance of P.F.R.A., I understand.
-and they were through surveying before Christmas. They were supposed to give us some decision on the 15th of February, but we had nothing. On the 15th of March they promised and now it is the 26th of April and we had nothing yet. They tell us now that our maps are on print, and that is as far as we know yet.
In this connection I would suggest that here is an area that has already been surveyed for drainage. All that is needed is to move in and get immediate action to drain the land. This letter was from Mr. Oscar Carlson of Beynes, Saskatchewan. He is a councillor in that area.
I am just going to quote one short paragraph from another letter from Clarence B. Hill, reeve of the Martin municipality No. 122, near Moosomin. This area is suffering now for the third year in a row. He suggests something which could be done, and the suggestion could tie in with the letter I have just read from Mr. Carlson. The letter reads:
I would suggest the dominion government set up units of draining machinery consisting of a dragline, cat and dozer and a cat and scraper, say one unit to each two or three municipalities to be used only for draining work. This would reinstate soured land, bring it back into production and taxes, and help considerable towards building roads, once the sloughs and potholes are drained.
That is a concrete suggestion by Clarence Hill. I quote these letters because they come right from this area and emphasize the seriousness of the position, In addition they offer some concrete suggestions which could be applied immediately. Here is an area south of Moosomin which has been surveyed and is ready to go. All that is needed is to follow the suggestion made by Mr. Hill and get this machinery moved out there to work on drainage ditches.
Again I want to emphasize that we are not alarmists; we are not panicky. If I were able to quote these letters in their entirety you would see the pioneering spirit that these people have. They have been out there with their own tractors constructing drainage facilities. The roads are gone, their municipal funds are exhausted, and this spring people have actually been out there with shovels trying to open up drains because all the work they did last year with their own tractors fell in as a result of these heavy rains. They are trying to save the efforts of a lifetime. I would strongly urge

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson that whatever can be done should be done, as I know it will be, by both the provincial and federal governments.
I want to thank the Prime Minister for the assurance he gave that when all the information is in concerning the situation, an assessment will be made and whatever help it is possible to give will be given. Finally, may I say that I feel rather sorry for the Minister of Finance. He mentioned in that budget that the western wheat crop was one source of revenue, and this condition may interfere with his sincere efforts to balance our economy. I am sure the government will give every sympathetic consideration to the situation I have tried to present.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have already participated in this budget debate, Mr. Speaker, but I cannot miss this opportunity of endorsing what has been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, by my colleagues in this party and by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who have all expressed the view that the crisis which faces Saskatchewan is certainly the most serious we have had during the lifetime of any of us in this parliament.
The Minister of Finance, bringing down his budget for next year, indicated that he expected we would have a good crop on the prairies. Had that crop materialized it would have made a great difference in our economy. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce is incorrect in his conclusion that you cannot forecast a crop failure in May. When I was home at Easter the outlook was promising. They had had a very good stretch of weather and, had it continued, the land could have been seeded in that area. But as a result of the excessive moisture over a four-year period, the very heavy rainfall last year and the four inches of rain which descended in the last month, it now becomes impossible to seed a large percentage of the land in Mackenzie.
Hon. members have not appreciated the magnitude of this problem. Figures showing farm net income of 1954, which reached us a few days ago, reveal a very sharp drop in net income across Canada, from $2,154 million in 1951 to $1,923 million in 1952, then down to $1,699 million in 1953 and $1,125 million in 1954. This represents a drop of over a billion dollars since 1951. In other words farm net income is cut almost in half.
The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. McBain), who spoke a few moments ago, had something to say about the position of the tobacco farmers. I would point out, however, that no farmers have been hit as hard as the wheat


farmers. Farm income is down in all provinces, but in Saskatchewan our income has dropped from $565-5 million in 1952 to $126-5 million in 1954.
It is not easy for us to think in terms of millions, but if one could picture oneself having an income of $565-and that, by the way, is the income some Canadian families have-what would be his position if that income were reduced in three years to $126? Or, to multiply those figures by twenty, to give an income somewhat in line with what a member of parliament considers he should have, it would represent a drop from $11,310 to $2,530. If one has not had some practical experience in reduced incomes over a short period of time, then he has missed something. Our people in Saskatchewan during the years of depression, and again during the last years, have seen prices collapse, and bad weather conditions. Coupled with the excessive rainfall last year we had heavy rust damage, which normally would not have developed had we not had so much wet weather,- or had more sunshine.
Those on farms, whose incomes have been reduced from $11,310 to $2,530, are in a position where they cannot pay their store bills, their taxes, or their commitments to the implement dealers. Payments to doctors fall in arrears. We have had a combination of these factors. I find that municipalities in my constituency, which had a very good record during the thirties and where we have always had some crop, reported tax arrears of $853,000 at the end of 1953. By the end of 1954 those arrears had reached $1,362,000.
People in Saskatchewan, as in other provinces, realize that if taxes get out of control they are in danger of losing their equity in their holdings, and no one accepts that position cheerfully. As a result of the fall in farm income, tax arrears have piled up. In addition to the tax arrears of the municipalities, the school districts find the municipalities owe them $1,170,000. The banks have been good enough to give the school units credit. Those school units in my district owed the banks over $844,000. Fortunately the banks have confidence in the province. However, this represents a tremendous waste, which is accepted unwillingly by the taxpayers, when such large amounts are paid out in interest. If they had had their fair share of the national income their taxes would have been paid and the school districts would have received their fair share of moneys.
I realize some hon. members from other parts of Canada are under the impression that those of us who come from the prairies do a good deal of complaining, and that at times we make unreasonable demands on the

taxpayers in other parts of Canada. I would remind the house, however, that in years of prosperity we in Saskatchewan are very glad to pay to the Minister of National Revenue a very generous share of our total income, through the income tax. I find that in the last publication of taxation statistics for 1954 a review is made of the year 1952. I was informed by the income tax branch this morning that they will not have information concerning the 1953 position until late in July, although they are speeding up the reporting of those amounts.
However, if one takes the total paid in income tax by the farmers of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta and adds them together, he gets less than the amount paid by Saskatchewan farmers in 1952. Farmers in all provinces of Canada, with the exception of British Columbia and Saskatchewan, paid $13,106,000 in 1952, whereas the farmers of Saskatchewan paid $13,268,000.
As I have said, the Saskatchewan farmers made no complaint about paying over $13 million into the treasury in 1952. Oh, some of them felt that it was hard to justify the fact that the farmers of the rich provinces of Ontario and Quebec paid less than $3 million when more than $13 million had been paid by farmers in Saskatchewan who, unfortunately, had not been able to build up a reserve for an emergency. I submit, therefore, that as a result of the net farm income of Saskatchewan dropping from $566 million in 1952 to $126 million in 1954 we have a matter of national concern, apart altogether from the disastrous weather we have experienced in the last month. When Professor Harrington estimates that this unusual weather will result in a reduction in income of over $50 million I am convinced that he is estimating on the conservative side.
By the end of this year the Minister of Finance will realize that the figures he had before him when he prepared his budget for this year did not take into account the fact that at the present time there is still some 1953 grain in the granaries of Saskatchewan. The minister is not really in a position to know the serious impact on our Canadian economy that last year's crop imposed. Many regions in Saskatchewan are in the position that now, on the 11th day of May, the water level is so high there is not a chance in the world of getting on the land to seed oats, barley, wheat or any of the cereals that have been grown in the prairie provinces.
This crisis is going to affect eastern Canada also. On our farm we spent a considerable sum of money last winter to buy
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson fertilizer. We expected that there would be a short growing season this year on account of the excessive moisture, and that if we were to have any crop we should use fertilizer to make the best use of the growing season. It is extremely doubtful whether we shall decide to lose the money that we have now invested in fertilizer, or hold it over for another year. Certainly it is going to have a very direct effect on the fertilizer industry in British Columbia and on the railway companies that transport fertilizer and other products from the west and the east to the prairie provinces.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) suggested that in addition to helping to meet the capital costs of the recent flooding, the federal government should somehow or other get into the pockets of the farmers whose fields will not be seeded at least $10 for every such acre. It is estimated that this year we shall have at least 2 million acres unseeded. The sum of $20 million may appear to be a large amount; but on the other hand, when one considers the importance of the wheat economy to the whole of Canada it is pretty obvious that sooner or later we shall have to face some of these problems and view them from the national point of view.
I should like to remind the house that late in the last century and in the beginning of this century, the prairie lands of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta were opened up for settlement on the theory that there would be a market for foodstuffs grown in the prairie provinces and shipped abroad. During my lifetime we have brought increased acreage into cultivation; we have improved our techniques of cultivation; we have brought down our costs of operation so that we are now in a position to produce great quantities of a very desirable commodity. We are compelled to sell in world markets in competition with other countries which, for a variety of reasons, are making it very difficult for Canadian grain to be sold.
Hon. members will perhaps have noted in this morning's Gazette that the United States now buys its own exports. That is to be found on the editorial page. It mentions that on May 2 the export-import bank in the United States made funds available to six manufacturing companies to help them export their products. This makes a total of 66 manufacturing firms which are being assisted by all of the manufacturers in the United States.
The hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) pointed out the very real problem that exists in his area where running shoes that were manufactured to the extent
3676	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson of 6 million in 1947 were manufactured to the extent of 2 million in 1954. That poses a problem not only for the hon. member for Waterloo North but for Canada. If our products have to compete in world markets with such products from other countries; if the Americans are going to use public funds to enable their manufacturers to sell their goods in world markets, it poses a real problem for us.
The editorial also mentions that last month the United States government offered Denmark $7 * 7 million worth of supplies, provided that Denmark would send industrial products to underdeveloped countries. Apparently Denmark objected to a clause which required the grain to be moved in United States vessels. But the shipment of $7-7 million worth of grain from the United States to Denmark will certainly affect the market in Denmark, and will eventually affect markets which we have had abroad.
I come back to our theories, which I think are fundamental. The 15 million people in Canada should be able somehow or other to organize our economy so we can produce all the food we can use-and we should produce all that we can-but we should be willing to exchange our foodstuffs in the markets of the world for commodities which other people have and which they would prefer to exchange for our foodstuffs. We should also make available, from our surplus supplies, foodstuffs for the two-thirds of the people in the world who never get enough to eat.
Therefore I suggest that the Minister of Finance, along with his colleagues, must give consideration to the request which has come from Saskatchewan that the emergency which has been created by the flooding be regarded as a national emergency, and that sufficient public funds be made available to help repair the property damage. Those who have invested their lives in Saskatchewan to produce food for ourselves and for our overseas markets should be given the assistance necessary over a series of years such as those we have experienced.
During the drought years federal and provincial governments joined with the municipalities in facing that problem. Last fall I met a number of my constituents who went north during the drought years, and they said they never expected to live long enough to be terrified when it started to rain. They had thought if they could only get to a country where they would have rain their troubles would be over; but after the experience they had last year they have come to the conclusion that the hardships involved in connection with a series of flooding are


even more difficult than the calamity which befell them during the 1930's, when it failed to rain and they were unable to grow a crop.
There is probably very little difference between a succession of crop failures as a result of drought and a series of crop failures as a result of flooding. However, there is this difference. In the years when you have flooding you have additional expenses that cannot be avoided very well. Last year a great many farmers spent more than the worth of their crop in trying to get on the fields with a combine towed by a caterpillar tractor. Sometimes it was a combine mounted on a stone boat, with a small engine to operate the combine, while the whole equipment was hauled around by a caterpillar tractor. The cost involved exceeded the revenue from the crop. So it makes very little difference whether a serious crop failure results from flooding or from drought.
I think it is obvious that the people of Canada as a whole must be prepared to stand behind the people of Winnipeg, of the Fraser valley, of the Annapolis valley, of Rimouski when disaster hits those areas, and likewise this year behind the people of the prairie provinces who are faced with disastrous floods. I am sure the government will only be fulfilling its duties to Canada in doing everything that is reasonably possible.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish at this time to bring to the attention of the government and the house a particular problem with which we are confronted in the Fraser valley. Some repetition may be necessary, but I shall try to present the matter as briefly and as quickly as possible. When participating in the throne speech debate I paid some attention to various fisheries problems, and endeavoured to place on the record not just my own views with respect to these matters but more especially the views of many of those engaged in the industry who are adversely affected by the imposition of certain measures which, these fishermen claim, are ineffective.
No doubt the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) works under a long range policy, and rather than just leaving this matter I thought if it were brought to his attention he might somehow or other work it into that long range policy and bring certain benefits to the fishermen in my area.
The annual list of proposals for changes in British Columbia fisheries regulations sent out from the office of Mr. A. J. Whitmore, chief supervisor of fisheries, under date of December 3, 1953, contained a clause having

to do with fishing above the New Westminster bridge. This clause No. 5 reads:
To prohibit commercial fishing above New Westminster bridge on and after September 16 each season.
Immediately after that was circulated various fishermen's groups took exception to it and lodged their protests against including this in the list of proposed changes in the fisheries regulations. The united fishermen and allied workers' union lodged a protest, as did the Pacific fishermen and allied trades union, gill net section. Just about that time, on March 16, 1954, I directed a question on the orders of the day to the Minister of Fisheries. The question, reported on page 3029 of Hansard, was as follows:
Will the minister state whether or not a decision has been reached with respect to the closure of the Fraser river above the New Westminster bridge to commercial fishing?
The answer I received from the minister on that occasion was as follows:
The answer to his question is no. I hope to be able to announce a decision before I meet the fishermen's union in convention next week in Vancouver.
Upon his return from Vancouver the minister made a statement with respect to this matter, to be found on page 4510 of Hansard of May 7, 1954, as follows:
I announced to the fishermen at the union meeting in Vancouver that we would stop that fishery on September 16.
And a little further on:
I met the union, I met the gill netters, I met the local mayors and reeves and pointed out that we were interested in quality and conservation.
And again:
Since I came back to Ottawa we have discussed the matter again with our research people and our officers, and it is probably right that we are doing it in a little too big a sweep. Therefore we have changed the closing date this year from September 16 to three weeks later, October 8. They will have the tail end of the sockeye and the first of the pinks and the chums. The hon. member for New Westminster applauds. I want to tell the committee that next year it will be September SO and the year after it will be September 15 because it is felt that in the interests of quality and conservation we must close this fishery. But because of the reasons put forward by these people for a little more gradual closing off, we have agreed to make that change.
Perhaps with some optimism, but prompted by the minister's co-operative attitude and his encouraging announcement, I ventured to express the hope that progressively earlier closures as threatened would be found unnecessary. However, that has not worked out and we find that the department are intent on continuing with their announced policy.
Further protests have been registered in this connection. I received one dated May
The Budget-Mr. Patterson 27, 1954, from the united fishermen and allied workers' union, the first part of which reads: Dear Sir,
We are enclosing with this letter copy of a letter just recently sent to the Hon. James Sinclair, Minister of Fisheries. You will note that we take quite sharp objection to a number of statements which he made in the House of Commons on May 7.
The most immediate issue is that of the closure of the area between Pattullo bridge and Mission bridge on the Fraser river. You will recall that on previous occasions we have written you at some length in respect to this proposed closure. Our members are not at all satisfied with the new revised decision which was announced by the minister. We urge you, as a member representing British Columbia, to do everything in your power to have the entire order rescinded.
That is just the first part of the letter which is signed by Homer Stevens, secretary treasurer of the union. Another communication which I received is in the form of a resolution dealing with fishing in the upper Fraser, adopted at a mass meeting in Fort Langley on Friday, October 8, 1954. It reads:
Whereas the 1954 salmon season is not a pink year as far as the Fraser river is concerned and
Whereas there is no dispute in quality of salmon in the Fraser river for the balance of the 1954 season and
Whereas we are fully aware of the fact that there is too much fishing gear in the water and therefore drastic conservation measures are necessary
Therefore be it resolved that we petition the Minister of Fisheries, Mr. Sinclair, to open the Fraser river again from the Pattullo bridge to Mission bridge as in past and that for the balance of the 1954 salmon season the minister is assured that we are escaping any conservation measures that may be necessary other than a complete closure; and
Be it further resolved that as far as the 1955 fishing season is concerned, further meeting be held with the minister in order that we may arrive at an equitable solution to this pertinent problem for the future.
Resolution carried unanimously.
Pete Jenewein acting as secretary.
Those are only two communications in this connection. The Pacific fishermen and allied trades union's brief of December 1 of last year raised a similar protest. A letter dated February 14, from the native sons of British Columbia, post No. 2, submitted a resolution in protest against this measure. I also have another communication from prevost post No. 10 of the native sons of British Columbia, dated January 4, 1955, which deals with the matter very fully and not only protests against the action that has been taken but asks that it be rescinded and proposes some other measures in its place.
Just prior to coming to this session of parliament, Mr. Speaker, we had the opportunity of meeting two delegations of fishermen, and they also registered their protest

The Budget-Mr. Patterson
over the measures proposed by the Minister of Fisheries. They presented statements showing that, as far as the purposes of these proposed measures were concerned, they were not being realized and they therefore felt that in all fairness the minister should rescind his proposed measure and take some more appropriate action in regard to conservation and so on.
There were two main reasons for the introduction of these measures. We find outlined in the British Columbia fishery regulations the suggested regulatory and administrative changes. We find these two are outlined very clearly, but I may say that the fishermen's unions take exception to both counts. In regard to conservation, I should like to read from article No. 5 of the suggested amendments to the British Columbia fishery regulations:
(b) the inability of the slow moving later classes of salmon, principally pinks and chums, to clear through the 50 mile stretch of the Fraser from its mouth to Mission during the protection period provided by the weekly closed times.
In this connection the brief has this to say:
It is represented the proposal would assist in meeting the difficulty and in addition would serve to give badly needed protection to spawning stocks of pinks and chums destined for important streams flowing into the Fraser between New Westminster and Mission, i.e., Coquitlam, Alouette, Whonock, Stave and Silverdale streams on the north side, and Salmon, Beaver, West, and other smaller creeks on the south side.
This was the position set out in this brief. The union's view in this connection is that the closure measures have not resulted in the desired and anticipated results. The brief has this to say:
We note that It is suggested that the closure of this area would help to rehabilitate several streams on the north and south sides of the Fraser river. Several points are not taken into consideration with regard to these streams.
After listing changed conditions on some of these tributaries, the brief goes on to state:
The fact of the matter is that as far as the local streams mentioned are concerned, the salmon have a better opportunity of entering these streams today than they had years ago when there were considerably less restrictions on fishing and it should be quite clear to everyone that the fine escapement of pinks to the upper Fraser river in 1953 passed the mouths of these streams en route.
With regard to the inability of the spawning fish to reach the headwaters of the main stem of the Fraser river, this particular brief contends that the escapement of the Fraser river pink salmon to the spawning ground in the last year was exceptionally good, and at least equal to any pink run in the last 40 years. It goes on to quote from the Department of Fisheries 1953 spawning

report dealing with the pinks in the Fraser river area. I should like to give this quotation from the same brief:
In 1951 we had no special closures on pink salmon fishing and the Department of Fisheries spawning report (1953) from which we quote does not bear out the contention that the closing of the fishing area above New Westminster bridge is necessary from a standpoint of conservation.
One of the other reasons given for the application of these earlier closures was the increasing efficiency of gill net operations through the use of nylon gear, etc. But the fishermen in this area maintain that the nylon nets have not proven as effective in this area in question as they have in other areas. They say it is due to the discolouration of the water in the Fraser river.
We also notice that in the minister's statement from which I have read there is reference to the necessity for these closures because of the quality of the fish. Some time ago I placed on record two letters, and I should like to refer to them again today. These letters have to do with the question of the quality of the fish taken in this area. The first one is to the Johnston Fishing and Packing Company, R.R.l, New Westminster, British Columbia. It is signed by Mr. Rolley. It reads as follows:
Gentlemen:
The directors of the gill net section of our union are desirous of obtaining information as to the procedure used in handling salmon caught above New Westminster bridge. As you probably know, there have been a lot of loose statements as to the quality of salmon caught in this area and in order to arrive at the facts of the case we would be very much obliged if your company could answer the questions listed below.
1.	In deliveries of salmon from your collectors to your plant are the salmon caught and collected above New Westminster bridge kept entirely separate at all times from salmon caught and collected in other parts of district No. 1.
2.	In the process of canning salmon at your plant is a separate code mark used to differentiate between salmon caught above New Westminster bridge and salmon caught in other parts of district No. 1?
3.	Does the government laboratory require certification from your company as to the place of origin of any parcel of canned salmon submitted by your company for inspection?
I should like to quote from the answer, or the letter Mr. Rolley received in reply. The letter reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
Replying to yours of the 4th instant in which you ask four questions dealing with the Fraser river fishing operations, our answer to the first three is "no".
The fourth question was:
4.	What percentage of this year's total pack was of grade B quality which was canned at your plant?
The reply to that fourth question was "none". I just place that information on the

record once again, Mr. Speaker, in order to show that the argument that has been used with respect to the quality of the salmon is not very conclusive.
I should like to refer just briefly to the economic effects of this broad measure. We find that the number of fishermen in this area taking out licences in 1953 stood at 639. I should like to emphasize the fact that these are gill net fishing licences. We further note that, in order to secure such a licence, the applicant must be a resident of that area. We therefore see that this is a considerable number who are affected at the present time and who will be affected by the earlier closures on the Fraser river.
As to the estimated loss, it is difficult, of course, to estimate that. We find that these fishermen through the years have adapted their boats and their fishing gear to local conditions. It would, of course, entail a heavy expenditure, estimated from $2,000 to $7,000 per boat, to convert their equipment for operation in other fishing areas. Of course that would be almost impossible for a great number of these fishermen. Then we also realize that if 639 fishermen are adversely affected by these closures, certainly the merchants of the area would suffer loss of income resulting from this measure.
I refer not only to these aspects of the problem, but I should like to remind the house that a considerable number of these people are veterans, I understand. I have here in my hand an article from the Gazette, Maple Ridge-Pitt Meadows, dated March 10, 1955. The article is headed "Canadian Legion Rap Proposed Closure of Fraser to Fishing. Charge Action is Drastic, Deprives Veterans of Jobs", and reads as follows:
Following a series of meetings between Canadian Legion officers from Haney, Mission and Agassiz, a resolution will be presented to the members of the organization protesting the closing of the Fraser river to commercial fishermen.
The resolution is expected to be approved by the memberships by a clear majority since it affects an estimated 105 veterans of the last war and first world war, presently engaged in fishing as a livelihood.
"Most of the equipment owned by the fishermen here is inadequate for fishing in the mouth of the Fraser or at sea", stated secretary-manager Roger Ansell of the Haney Legion branch.
Following is the resolution to be presented to the memberships of three valley Legion branches and then forwarded to the federal government. Department of Fisheries.
Whereas the federal Department of Fisheries has decided to close the Fraser river to commercial fishermen on September 16, 1955, from Pattullo bridge, New Westminster to Mission city;
And whereas the Minister of Fisheries has definitely stated this is the first step towards the complete closure of this area to commercial fishing;
And whereas the chief reason given for this drastic action is to maintain and increase the conservation of salmon, a statement strongly disputed by fishermen;
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
And whereas this drastic and unwarranted action will undoubtedly deprive many veterans of world wars I and II who have a large investment in equipment and through age and disability, though able to fish in home waters cannot stand the rigours of going upcoast in open waters to make their livelihood;
Be it resolved that the B.C. and N.W.S. command of the Canadian Legion register the strongest possible protest directly to the Minister of Fisheries against the closure of the Fraser river to commercial fishing in this area.
In an effort to evaluate the amount of loss that will occur to the fishermen if the river is closed permanently, the legion are presently circulating questionnaires to the fishermen in each area.
The questionnaire contains ten pertinent questions such as age, service record, length of fishing activities, home ownership, veterans allowances for purchase of home or equipment, equipment owned, such as boat gear, float or dockage and net shed, value of these and whether the fisherman is capable of supporting himself outside the industry and his physical capabilities.
Then the article concludes with this paragraph:
It is expected that a compilation of the information so gathered will be presented with the resolution as a brief.
I give that quotation in order to indicate that, as is brought out in that brief, about 105 veterans of the first and second world wars will be adversely affected.
Some of the suggested alternate proposals that we find in these various briefs are the following. The first is a treaty with the United States covering conservation of pink runs and equal catch division. In this connection, on page 7 of a brief dated February 5, 1954, sent to Mr. A. J. Whitmore, chief supervisor of fisheries, Department of Fisheries, Vancouver, we find this statement:
Certain things stand out like a sore thumb. The Americans are getting 65 per cent of the Fraser pink catch, the Canadian fleet as a whole is getting about 35 per cent. Out of the total run, the fishermen in area 29D are getting about 1 per cent. Out of the Canadian portion, they are only getting about 3 per cent. Even out of the Fraser river area catch they only took about 12 per cent. Yet it is suggested that closure of this area after September 16th would help solve the difficult problerp of pink conservation.
The second suggestion I have gleaned from these briefs is the equalization of the weekend closures between the approaches to the Fraser and the Fraser river, combined with a deliberate program of equalizing catches between Canadian seiners and gill netters; third, the extension of weekly closures if advisable; and fourth, reappraisal of the whole situation with respect to closure measures.
Just to sum up this matter, Mr. Speaker, I have intimated first of all that the fishermen still maintain that the measures' that have been put into operation are largely ineffective. Second, the efficiency of the new

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny gear is overestimated so far as the Fraser river is concerned. Third, the quality argument used by the Minister of Fisheries is not conclusive. Fourth, the displacement of fishermen from this area is too high a price for any slight possible results. Fifth, the financial loss is not justified. Finally, I would say that more effective and less discriminatory measures are possible in the solution of the problem of conservation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not my
intention, Mr. Speaker, to delay the house very long, but I do wish to refer briefly to a matter which I believe is of extreme importance. It is important from the point of view of the political conduct of those who are in charge of our affairs, and also from the point of view of administration.
On two occasions during this session I have raised questions in the house in connection with the Department of National Revenue concerning certain tax remissions being made by that department to certain corporations. On the second occasion we were promised an explanation by the minister. May I say incidentally, sir, that I have notified the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) that I am raising this matter in the house this afternoon. Unfortunately he is not in his seat, but perhaps he will be in later.
While we are still waiting for the answer to that question, another has come up that has to do with the same department. I believe it is time a statement was made in the house to set out all the facts in order that we can be sure the law of the land is being observed. In order to put the background of this question as fairly as possible, I should like to quote part of an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Star today. It deals with the question of Mr. Dempsey and the connection his activities have had with the Minister of National Revenue and others. The editorial reads as follows:
Mr. Dempsey admits that at least $5,000 in 1951 election funds, contributed to him by the late John Drohan, were not reported to the returning officer as required by the Ontario election act. The act provides penalties for failing to make a detailed statement of campaign fund receipts, and for making a false return. In Mr. Dempsey's case, penalties upon conviction might total more than $13,000.
Then the editorial continues with a reference to a statement made by the attorney general of Ontario, which appeared in the same newspaper. The statement was to the effect that no action would be taken, and the editorial continues as follows:
But Mr. Dana Porter, attorney general in the Frost government, says he has no intention of laying a charge against Mr. Dempsey. Does this mean that Conservative candidates in Ontario can

flout the election act with impunity and feel safe from prosecution in the courts as long as their government is in power?
The widow of the late Mr. Drohan says he told her he handed over the money to Mr. Dempsey "for favours he would get from the government". Perhaps the attorney general prefers to have Mr. Dempsey escape all penalty rather than have the facts brought out in court.
It is up to the voters in the June 9 election to judge as to what standard of political morality prevails in Ontario government circles. It is bad enough that highway frauds, irregularities and overpayments totalled many millions in a few years; that thousands of dollars were contributed to a Conservative candidate in advance for concessions expected from the lands and forests department. But it is worse still when the government deliberately does its best to prevent the public getting all the facts.
Up to that point I agree with the Toronto Star that it is a matter for the consideration of the Ontario electors whenever they have to cast their ballots. This is the part to which I wish to address myself particularly, because this goes much farther than Ontario. The last part says:
The Renfrew South election fund scandal came to light only by accident through receipts in the estate of the donor, who died in 1952. The voters have the right to wonder how many other government candidates benefited in similar fashion through large contributions which will never be revealed. Certain it is that the Ontario Conservative party never seems to lack for funds at election time.
May I add to that my opinion that the Liberal party does not seem to lack for election funds, either in Ontario or elsewhere. The reason this involves the House of Commons is that we are all trustees of the public treasury. It is true that for the time being the Minister of National Revenue is in charge of and responsible for the collection of the taxes imposed by this parliament. Since we are the public representatives it is we, in the last analysis, who are the final trustees of the public purse. Any time there appears to be any irregularity affecting moneys which are the property of the people of Canada, then the representatives of the people have a right to know the full facts and have a full explanation laid before them in order that they may be able to explain to their electors just what is happening.
I believe the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) performed a public service when on May 9 of this year he asked the following question on the orders of the day, which appears at page 3565 of Hansard:
In view of the speculation raised by an editorial in today's Globe and Mail regarding the minister's previous knowledge of the Dempsey affair, will the minister clarify the situation by making a statement to the house?
That was a very fair question. I think he gave the minister a wonderful opportunity to lay the facts before the house. What did

we get at that time? The reply was that the minister was prohibited by section 133 of the Income Tax Act and section 55 of the succession duty act-I believe that section number should have been different- from disclosing the information he had. He did admit in his reply, and I quote:
I admit that I had a conference with Mr. Frost while he was in Ottawa. He had to leave hurriedly, so that the conference was incomplete. I am not in a position to disclose any information that passed between us at that time.
The question was followed up later by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), when he asked if the minister could point out where, in section 133 of the Income Tax Act, the minister found authority under which he could disclose information to Premier Frost which he could not disclose to parliament. The reply given to that was:
I quoted section 133 with reference to the Income Tax Act and section 54 of the succession duty act, and it was under section 55 of the succession duty act that Premier Frost, as treasurer of Ontario, was entitled to any information we have.
We go to section 55 of the succession duty act, and what do we find? I shall quote the whole section because it is short, at least the first part of the section which has to do with this matter.
55. (1) No person employed in the service of Her Majesty shall communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto, any information obtained under the provisions of this act, or allow any such person to inspect or have access to any written statement furnished under the provisions of this act.
Quite obviously the minister is attempting to justify the result on the basis of these words, "any person not legally entitled thereto", and perhaps is prepared to argue that in his opinion the premier of Ontario was so entitled. But is it not a strange situation, where one would expect that the persons entitled to that information would be officials of the department-and one would expect that those officials are sworn to secrecy; because if they are not, then this whole section becomes a farce and means nothing-if one person, who is bound by the secrecy of the act, gives information to somebody else who is not so bound? If that is so, then of course the act has no effect.
I would ask the Minister of National Revenue to state in this house whether he considers Premier Frost in the same category as officials of his own department, and whether Premier Frost is sworn to secrecy under the provisions of the Income Tax Act. If that is not the case; if Premier Frost is not in the same category as officials of the Department of National Revenue and the minister himself, then of course he is not
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny subject to the same restrictions. The minister, then, had no business to disclose information to a person who is not bound by the secrecy provision, when he has refused to give the same information, or similar information, in the House of Commons.
What makes the matter still worse is this, that if what I am now going to quote is correct, then of course the whole thing becomes a sort of midsummer night's dream.
I quote now from the report of a speech made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees), as it is reported in the Ottawa Citizen of today:
Revenue Minister McCann was charged today with playing politics with the Dempsey case and of withholding information from Premier Frost of Ontario until he felt it would be of political advantage to have it known.
George Hees, president of the national Progressive Conservative association and M.P. for Toronto-Broadview told a regional party meeting here the method chosen by Dr. McCann to communicate the information by drawing the premier into a corner at the recent federal-provincial meeting "was just like a Parisian postcard vendor trying to peddle his wares".
Well, I am not going to say that I agree with that description of the way in which this information was given, because I have nothing to base it upon; but certainly it appears as if the Minister of National Revenue were trying to make a sort of cloak and dagger affair out of the whole matter. If the information which came to the notice of the minister as the result of the administration of an estate-and we are given to understand that this happened a few years ago-was in his possession, and if he felt that the law of the land was being broken, or that regulations were not being lived up to, then it was his duty at that time to notify the proper authorities.
If he felt that it was an evasion of the Income Tax Act, and that undisclosed income was involved, then I think it was his duty to lay a proper charge and start action at that time. The fact that he did not do so lends credence to the statement made by the president of the Progressive Conservative association.
The part that really causes me the greatest concern is this. Further on in the same report it is stated that Mr. Dempsey, in speaking to a reporter today, is credited with having said that he had not reported his contribution to the 1951 campaign funds, because-and these are the words in the report-
-he had received assurances from revenue minister J. J. McCann that income tax authorities would take no action on the matter.

speechtext:
Absolutely false.

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then there is this further direct quotation:
"Just mind your P's and Q's and the government won't do anything about the contribution," Mr. Dempsey said he was told by Dr. McCann.
I say this, that if those words are correct then the Minister of National Revenue, in fairness to himself and in fairness to this parliament, should forthwith hand in his resignation because any minister-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. member disagrees he will have an opportunity to say so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wish at this time to declare positively that the statement you have just quoted is absolutely false in every particular.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I take it that the minister refers to the last quotation I put on the record. He did not identify which one. If that is not correct, then of course the minister and Mr. Dempsey can fight that out between themselves. The fact remains that in my opinion there has been a lack of frankness on the part of the minister. If the minister obtained certain information-and we are given to understand that it was as the result of his being a director of a company which had something to do with the administration of an estate-which he felt was evidence of a law being violated, and if he withheld that information from the appropriate sources for two or three years in order to use it for political purposes, that in itself in my opinion would be enough for the minister to be charged with a great misdemeanour.
It is not the prerogative or the right of a minister of the crown to use his position for political purposes, particularly a position such as that held by the Minister of National Revenue, who has access to information so confidential that even when it affects the public interest he will not disclose it to parliament because, he tells us, the secrecy provisions of the act do not permit him to do so. I say that to use that kind of information for political purposes is in my opinion a dereliction of duty and an abuse of public trust. If the minister has used his position, either as director of a company or as Minister of National Revenue, to obtain information and hold it for a strategic time at which he could do political harm to his opponent, then I say he is performing an act for which he should be censured.
I say that very frankly, because I am not at all satisfied that the Minister of National Revenue has given the house any information so far. The questions that have been put to him and the answers we have received have left much to be desired. It is still 

not clear, certainly not to me, what the minister means when he tells us that under section 55 of the Dominion Succession Duty Act he is permitted to give information to the premier of Ontario. When he says that, then I think the minister should state in this house how he comes to that conclusion.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is treasurer of Ontario.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the premier of Ontario an official of the minister's department? Is he sworn to secrecy, so far as this act is concerned? That is what I want to know.
Point 2 is this. Did the minister have this information for the last two or three years as a result of the fact that he was director of a company and, if so, why did he not give that information to the proper authorities and see that appropriate action was taken?
While we are on this subject, may I say that a new method seems to be creeping in. There was a time when the Prime Minister of Canada used to insist that ministers of the crown should divest themselves of directorships in companies. Apparently a change has come about, and we now have the new look in government. They can have one foot in the government and one foot in private business and use both sources to advantage, one for the other.
I hope that process has not gone too far, because it makes one wonder to what extent it could be used if ministers of the crown were to find themselves in the position of obtaining confidential information from private industry, on the one hand and, on the other hand, in the position of being able to obtain private and confidential information in a government position. One can easily imagine the terrific abuses that could creep into the administration of the affairs of this country if that were so.
I think it is time the Minister of National Revenue gave the House of Commons the facts and explained why, if he had information which came to him as the result of a position he holds outside the government and which he felt perfectly willing to give to the premier of Ontario a few weeks ago, he kept that information hidden all this time; and whether there is any truth at all in the statement that he had assured Mr. Dempsey that the government would not take action with regard to the contribution in 1951.

He can tell the house exactly what has happened and where he finds authority in section 55 of the succession duty act to disclose information to the premier of Ontario which he cannot disclose to this house, and to what extent he is involved in this whole question of the contributions to Mr. Dempsey which came to his knowledge as a result of his being a director of the company.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Apparently the house is anxious to hear me, so I shall continue.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) told of some of the difficulties his people encounter in trying to carry on fishing in the Fraser river, as the result of certain action the Department of Fisheries has taken to conserve, or so-called conserve, salmon. I have a similar problem in my riding, and I should like to second everything that he has brought to the attention of the house.
I am sure the minister has had many representations, even as I and the hon. member for Fraser Valley have had. We have had many meetings; we have had many letters indicating disapproval of the regulation that was brought in a year ago announcing the date of closure of salmon fishing above the Pattullo bridge. Many cross words have been used and many accusations have been made.
The Budget-Mr. Hahn
The hon. member for Fraser Valley mentioned Peter Jenewein. He is a fisherman; he is connected with the united fishermen and allied workers' union. He is also the reeve of the municipal district of Maple Ridge. As recently as the day before this house opened he indicated to me that things had reached such a state between the Minister of Fisheries and the gill net fishermen that they considered it absolutely futile to talk to such an autocratic minister. Such a condition is most unfortunate. It is most unfortunate that any group of producers in this country should feel it absolutely futile to spend a few moments with a minister of the crown discussing the possibility of rectifying a condition that has been forced upon them. I would say that some fault must lie with the minister.
The history of the fishing industry in British Columbia is long, and I do not intend to elaborate on it at this time. However, last year the minister indicated something of the story of the protection of the sockeye salmon industry in British Columbia, and what it means to that province. I am not too interested in that question at this time, by reason of the fact that the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, which was set up some years ago to protect the sockeye salmon, has done an excellent job on the conservation of sockeye. Last year we had the finest sockeye salmon fishing season in the history of our province. We obtained something in the neighbourhood of 9,500,000 salmon. This commission, which is virtually a partnership between United States and Canadian fishermen, has proven most successful, with the result that an industry that at one time was threatened with extinction is today thriving.
I should like the minister to recognize one fact in this regard. That is that we built up a tremendous fishing industry because we had conservation of fish according to the proposals set forth by the fishermen themselves under the international joint commission which studied the question. Fishing was continued above the Pattullo bridge, the very thing the minister is asking us not to do today. The conservation program that was carried out under the terms of the agreement helped to save our sockeye fishing industry.
The fishermen themselves are most anxious to protect their own industry. They know what will happen to them unless they have conservation in all branches of the fishing industry, so they have done everything possible to study the question. They have tried to meet the minister half way, but it

The Budget-Mr. Hahn seems that such a thing is quite impracticable and the minister just will not listen.
When the minister spoke in the debate last year he indicated that he had changed his mind to a certain extent, and he set back the time for closure by some six weeks. He mentioned at that time that it would gradually be closed off completely. However, that is not desirable. It did not satisfy the gill netters, who are most affected by this particular action.
The representations that were made to the minister by the united fishermen and allied workers' union, as well as by the gill net section of the Pacific fishermen and allied trades union, were mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Fraser Valley and I am not going to deal with them at this time.
